meta.title: No Budget
meta.subtitle: The Underground Playbook for Negotiating When They Claim They Can't Pay
meta.description: 15 moves for the negotiation that starts after they say no. Read the signal, shift the frame, make the case, and know when to walk.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: "No Budget" Means "Not Yet" or "Not You"
cards.hook: They said 'no budget.' That's not a wall. It's a question in disguise.
cards.truth:
Most people fold when they hear 'no budget.' That's exactly what the other side wants.
• 'No budget' hides three different problems — timing, priority, or missing authority.
• Once you know which one, the next move becomes obvious.
• Treating all three the same kills deals that aren't actually dead.
cards.remember: Find out which kind of no you're hearing before you do anything else.
cards.theySee: A vendor who stops pushing and nods politely after hearing the word 'budget.'

signals.t: They say 'maybe next quarter' — the money exists but isn't available right now.
They mention the CFO or a committee — they're telling you they don't decide.
They say 'it's just not in the cards' — they're deflecting, not explaining.
They move to something else right after saying no — they don't want to be questioned.

steps.title: Name the three types
steps.desc: Write down: timing, priority, authority. These are the only three real reasons behind any 'no budget.'

steps.title: Ask which one it is
steps.desc: Say: 'When you say no budget — do you mean not now, or not this project?' Watch the answer closely.

steps.title: Route to the right move
steps.desc: Timing means ask when. Priority means make the urgency case. Authority means find who can actually say yes.

cards.script: "When you say no budget — do you mean not this quarter, or not this project?"
cards.counter:
Someone testing if you'll fold without a fight.
• Notice if they say 'no budget' with no date, no number, and no name attached.
• Say: 'When you say no budget — do you mean not now, or not this?'
• Wait for the answer. Their next sentence is your real information.
cards.insight: The harder part is staying quiet long enough to hear which no they meant — most people fill the silence with a price drop they didn't need to give.

cards.title: The Person Saying 'No Budget' May Not Control the Money
cards.hook: You're being rejected by someone who can't approve anything. That's not a rejection — it's a detour.
cards.truth:
Gatekeepers pass the objection their boss owns. It looks like a no, but it isn't theirs to give.
• They like your offer but still say no — the block isn't your pitch, it's their authority.
• Every minute you spend convincing them is time the real decision-maker doesn't know your name.
• Your move is to find the person who can actually move money — not the one who can't.
cards.remember: Stop selling to people who can't buy. Find the person who can.
cards.theySee: A salesperson still talking to the person who said no instead of asking who actually decides.

signals.t: They say 'it's out of my hands' — they're telling you they don't decide.
They like what you're offering but still say no — the block isn't your case.
One specific name keeps coming up — that person holds the money.
They describe multiple steps before anything gets approved — you're far from the top.

steps.title: Confirm their authority
steps.desc: Ask: 'Who else is part of this decision?' before you go any deeper into your pitch.

steps.title: Get the name
steps.desc: Ask: 'Who would need to be in the room for this to actually move?' Write the name down.

steps.title: Request the introduction
steps.desc: Say: 'Would you be willing to bring me into that conversation?' Don't make them the messenger.

cards.script: "Who else would need to be involved for this to actually move forward?"
cards.counter:
Someone redirecting you to a lower-level contact instead of the decision-maker.
• Notice if you've had two or more meetings without speaking to whoever approves spending.
• Say: 'I'd like to speak directly with whoever owns this decision.'
• If they refuse, treat the deal as not real until proven otherwise.
cards.insight: A gatekeeper can't say yes — but they can absolutely say no. The move that follows is making sure you're not building a case for someone who can only block.

cards.title: Map the Real Budget Before You Name Your Price
cards.hook: They haven't told you what they can spend. That doesn't mean they don't know.
cards.truth:
Clients hide their budget to keep room to negotiate. Most people name a price before knowing where the floor is.
• Ask about the project's financial goal — they'll answer that when they won't answer 'what's your budget.'
• 'What does a successful result need to pay back?' gets you a real number to work from.
• Once you know their expected return, your price becomes a fraction of it.
cards.remember: Ask about their goal first. Name your price second.
cards.theySee: A consultant asking detailed questions about the business before ever mentioning a number.

signals.t: They mention a growth target before you ask — they know their success number.
They say what a competitor charges — they've already researched the range.
They push you for a number before answering your questions — they want to anchor you first.
They can't describe the project clearly — they're testing whether you'll anchor low.

steps.title: Ask about the goal
steps.desc: Say: 'What does a successful version of this need to pay back for your business in the next 12 months?' Write the number.

steps.title: Do the math
steps.desc: Your price should be a clear fraction of their stated goal. Calculate it before you speak.

steps.title: Name your number second
steps.desc: Let them describe what success looks like, then anchor your price inside that context — not outside it.

cards.script: "What does a successful version of this need to pay back for your business in the next 12 months?"
cards.counter:
They're trying to anchor your price before you know their ceiling.
• Notice if they ask for a number before you've discussed scope or goals.
• Say: 'Help me understand what you're trying to achieve first.'
• Don't answer the price question until you know their success number.
cards.insight: The real trap is naming your price before you know their number — now they negotiate down from yours instead of up from theirs.

cards.title: "Can't Pay" Is a Choice, Not a Fact
cards.hook: 'We can't afford it' is not the same as 'there is no money.' One is a constraint. The other is a priority call.
cards.truth:
Money exists in almost every organization. The question is what it's currently going toward.
• 'Can't' means the money is already spent on something else — which means it can move.
• Find what they're paying for now. That's where your real budget conversation is.
• The move: turn 'do we have money' into 'is this the best use of what we have.'
cards.remember: There is no 'can't pay.' There is only 'we chose to spend it somewhere else.'
cards.theySee: A person calmly questioning the word 'can't' instead of accepting the rejection and preparing to leave.

signals.t: They mention a tool or vendor they currently pay — the budget exists, it's just elsewhere.
They get slightly prickly when you push on 'can't' — they know it's a choice.
They go quiet after you question the word — they're recalibrating their position.
They bought something else recently — the money was there and it moved somewhere.

steps.title: Question the word 'can't'
steps.desc: Say: 'When you say can't — do you mean the money doesn't exist, or it's already going somewhere else?'

steps.title: Find where the money went
steps.desc: Ask: 'What are you spending on right now that this would replace or reduce?' Listen for real numbers.

steps.title: Reframe it as a trade
steps.desc: Show them that buying you means stopping or reducing something else — not adding a brand new cost.

cards.script: "When you say can't — do you mean the money doesn't exist, or that it's already going somewhere else?"
cards.counter:
Someone testing how much pressure it takes before you drop your price.
• Notice if the word 'can't' appears with no specific explanation attached to it.
• Say: 'I understand — tell me what you're working with and we'll see what's possible.'
• Don't drop your number before they've explained what 'can't' actually means.
cards.insight: The harder part is that once they admit it's a choice, they own the decision — and some people would rather keep the excuse than make the call.

cards.title: Label the Fear Hidden Behind 'No Budget'
cards.hook: 'No budget' is almost never about money. It's about not wanting to be wrong in front of their team.
cards.truth:
The objection on the surface is price. The objection underneath is fear of making a bad call.
• Labeling the real fear disarms it faster than answering the price question.
• Say what they're likely feeling out loud — they'll confirm or correct you. Either way, you get closer.
• Once the fear is named, money becomes a logistics problem, not an emotional wall.
cards.remember: Say the fear out loud. That moves them faster than dropping your price.
cards.theySee: Someone sitting quietly and listening instead of jumping in to defend a price or offer a discount.

signals.t: They say 'we've been burned before' — past failure is making them hesitate right now.
They ask for case studies or references before moving — they need to feel safe first.
They seemed ready, then stalled — something shifted in how they're thinking about risk.
They keep saying 'we' instead of 'I' — they're afraid of being blamed by their team.

steps.title: Listen for the fear word
steps.desc: Write down the exact phrases they used. Look for risk language, mentions of past problems, or group blame.

steps.title: Name it back
steps.desc: Say: 'It sounds like you're worried this won't pay off and you'll have a hard time defending it internally.'

steps.title: Wait five seconds
steps.desc: Don't follow the label with more words. Sit in silence. Let them respond and correct or confirm you.

cards.script: "It sounds like you're worried this won't pay off and you'll have a hard time defending it to your team."
cards.counter:
Someone labeling your hesitation to pressure you into moving faster.
• Notice if they name a fear you haven't stated out loud yet.
• Correct it calmly: 'That's not quite it — the real issue is...' and name it yourself.
• Don't let them define your concern for you. Own the label or change it.
cards.insight: The move that follows is showing them what a bad decision looks like if they do nothing — so the fear of staying stuck gets bigger than the fear of spending.

cards.title: Get Them to Say No to the Worse Option
cards.hook: Stop pushing for yes. Get them to say no to the version they'd hate most.
cards.truth:
A calibrated no is easier to get than a yes — and it moves the deal forward just as well.
• Ask: 'Would it be a problem if nothing changed and things stayed exactly as they are?'
• They say no. That no is a quiet yes to doing something about the problem.
• Now the question isn't 'do you want to spend?' — it's 'what's the smallest version that avoids the bad result?'
cards.remember: A 'no' to the bad option is a yes to moving forward. Use it.
cards.theySee: A person asking an unexpected question instead of defending a price or pushing hard for a decision.

signals.t: They've described a clear problem or gap — they know what staying stuck looks like.
They keep delaying with no clear explanation — they're avoiding, not deciding.
They say 'we've managed this far' — they're telling you their bar is lower than they'll admit.
The mood in the room drops when the current situation gets named — they don't like it.

steps.title: Name the bad outcome
steps.desc: Ask: 'If this doesn't get solved, what does the next six months look like?' Let them describe it in full.

steps.title: Ask the calibrated no question
steps.desc: Say: 'Would it be a problem if nothing changed here and things stayed exactly as they are now?'

steps.title: Move to the minimum version
steps.desc: Once they say no to staying stuck, ask: 'What's the smallest version of this that avoids that result?'

cards.script: "Would it be a problem if nothing changed here and things stayed exactly as they are now?"
cards.counter:
Someone using this to make inaction feel scarier than their price.
• Notice if they describe a cost-of-inaction number without showing how they calculated it.
• Ask: 'What are the actual costs of the alternative you're describing? Walk me through that.'
• Make them show their math before you accept the framing.
cards.insight: This works until they realize you're running the move — so use their words to name the bad outcome, not yours.

cards.title: Show the Cost of the Problem Before You Show Your Price
cards.hook: Your price looks big when it's the only number in the room. Put a bigger number next to it first.
cards.truth:
People work harder to avoid a loss than to gain something equal in size. Documented and almost always ignored.
• Calculate what the problem is costing them monthly. Use their numbers, not yours.
• Put that cost on the table before you name your price.
• Now your price is the smaller number — and that's the only comparison that matters.
cards.remember: Show the cost of the problem before you show the cost of fixing it.
cards.theySee: Someone writing out the cost of the problem on a page before showing a price — doing math, not pitching.

signals.t: They've told you a revenue loss or time cost — they've already done part of the math for you.
They're relaxed about the problem — they haven't priced the pain yet.
They name a cheaper option — they're comparing price to price, not cost to cost.
They say 'we'll get to it eventually' — they haven't calculated what waiting actually costs.

steps.title: Ask for their loss number
steps.desc: Say: 'What is this problem costing you per month right now, roughly?' Wait for a number. Don't fill the silence.

steps.title: Do the math out loud
steps.desc: Say: 'So over six months, that's [X]. My price is [Y].' Then stop talking completely.

steps.title: Let silence work
steps.desc: Don't explain further after the comparison. Silence is where the decision forms. Hold it for as long as it takes.

cards.script: "What is this problem costing you per month right now — roughly?"
cards.counter:
Someone showing you a large cost-of-inaction number to justify their price.
• Ask: 'How did you calculate that?' Force them to show the math behind the figure.
• If they can't break it down, the number is a pressure move, not a fact.
• Build your own cost calculation using numbers you can verify independently.
cards.insight: The trap is when they don't know their own cost — now you're selling a solution to a problem they haven't priced, and that's a much harder conversation to close.

cards.title: Tie Your Price to a Number They Already Track
cards.hook: They don't know if your price is high or low. Give them a reference point they already trust.
cards.truth:
A price with no reference feels expensive. A price tied to a business goal feels like a decision.
• Find what a good result is worth to them — in revenue, deals closed, or cost avoided.
• Show your price as a small fraction of that number.
• Now they're not buying a service. They're buying a known return on a number they believe.
cards.remember: Every price looks big until you put their own goal number next to it.
cards.theySee: A vendor walking through math using the client's own business numbers instead of a standard rate card.

signals.t: They've named a revenue or growth target — that's your reference point right there.
They have a time-sensitive goal — attach your price to what missing the deadline costs them.
They describe what a competitor achieves that they don't — that gap has a dollar value.
They ask 'what kind of return can we expect?' — they already think in value terms.

steps.title: Get their success number
steps.desc: Ask: 'What would a successful version of this look like in dollars or deals over the next year?'

steps.title: Anchor your price to it
steps.desc: Say: 'My fee is [X]. If this works as designed, that's less than 10% of the upside you described.'

steps.title: Write the fraction down
steps.desc: Say it and write it. A 10:1 ratio changes the room. A number on paper is harder to argue with.

cards.script: "My fee is [X]. If this works as we've discussed, that's a small fraction of the upside you described — less than 10%."
cards.counter:
Someone tying their price to a return number they created without showing the source.
• Ask: 'How did you arrive at that upside figure?' Make them show the math.
• If they can't, the reference point is invented — not a real anchor.
• Propose your own return calculation using numbers you can independently verify.
cards.insight: The harder part is getting them to say the goal number out loud — people who won't name a target usually can't justify a decision in either direction.

cards.title: Never Apologize for Your Price
cards.hook: The second you soften your number, they start negotiating from the soft version. Name it flat and shut up.
cards.truth:
An apology on a price signals that the price is wrong. The other side hears permission to push harder.
• Name your price in one sentence with no hedge, no backstory, no 'I know it's a lot.'
• The urge to explain is fear. The other side can smell it from across the table.
• Silence after the number is your strongest move. Most people fill it with a discount they didn't need to give.
cards.remember: Say the number. Stop talking. The silence after is theirs to fill.
cards.theySee: Someone who names a price and sits back without flinching, adding qualifiers, or reaching for a discount.

signals.t: They go quiet after you name the number — this is normal. Don't fill it.
They say it with no real objection — they're testing whether you'll back down.
They wait silently after you speak — they expect you to soften the number next.
They move back in their chair after the number — they're thinking, not leaving.

steps.title: Write out your price sentence
steps.desc: Before any meeting, write: 'My fee for this is [X].' Nothing after the period. Practice saying it flat.

steps.title: Deliver it and stop
steps.desc: Say the sentence. Close your mouth. Count silently to 10 if you have to. Do not add anything.

steps.title: Let them go first
steps.desc: Whatever they say next is your real information. React to their words, not to the silence before them.

cards.counter:
They named a price and went quiet to force you to speak first.
• Notice the silence and don't fill it — they're using the same move on you.
• Name your counter if you have one, and deliver it just as flatly.
• If they're still silent after your counter, you've reached the real negotiation.
cards.insight: Most people lose money in the three seconds after saying a number. The move that follows is knowing exactly what to say when they finally do respond.

cards.title: Cut the Scope — Never Cut Your Rate
cards.hook: They want a lower number. Give them less work — not a cheaper rate. Your rate is not the thing that moves.
cards.truth:
Dropping your rate signals that your price was inflated. Dropping scope keeps the logic intact.
• Every rate cut tells them they were right to push — and that they can push again next time.
• A scope cut says: 'This is what that budget buys. Want more? The price goes back up.'
• You keep your rate, your positioning, and the door open for a bigger next engagement.
cards.remember: Drop what you deliver, not what you charge per hour or per day.
cards.theySee: A vendor calmly describing a smaller version of the project instead of getting defensive or cutting a rate.

signals.t: They give you a specific spending number — now you have something real to design around.
They say 'we don't really need X' — they're already thinking in scope terms.
They mention a cheaper competitor — ask what that option actually includes.
They want to move faster than the full project allows — the scope is already naturally smaller.

steps.title: Ask what they can spend
steps.desc: Say: 'What's the number you're working with?' Get a specific figure before you offer anything at all.

steps.title: Build the smaller version
steps.desc: List your three main deliverables. Circle the two that fit their budget. Name clearly what gets removed.

steps.title: Hold your rate
steps.desc: Say: 'At your budget, here's what I can deliver. The rate stays the same — the scope adjusts.'

cards.script: "At that budget, here's what I can deliver. The rate stays the same — we're adjusting what's in scope."
cards.counter:
Someone cutting scope on you while holding their rate.
• Ask: 'What does the full version include, and what's the price difference between the two?'
• Get the gap in writing before you agree to less work.
• Make sure what's being cut isn't something you need to make the rest of the project work.
cards.insight: The trap is that a smaller scope at your full rate still leaves them with a gap — and they'll ask you to fill it for free later. Define the edges in writing before you start.

cards.title: Offer a Payment Plan Before You Drop the Total
cards.hook: They say they can't pay your price. Most of the time, they mean they can't pay it all at once.
cards.truth:
Cash flow kills deals that budget doesn't actually block. A payment plan fixes cash flow — not the total.
• Splitting into three payments turns a large number into a manageable monthly line.
• The total doesn't change — but their approval process might not even require it to.
• This costs you nothing and saves deals that would otherwise die on timing alone.
cards.remember: Split the payments before you split the price.
cards.theySee: A vendor offering a payment option before the client has finished explaining why they can't pay.

signals.t: They say 'we just don't have it right now' — the timing is the issue, not the total.
They mention a budget cycle or fiscal quarter — cash timing is the real constraint.
They can approve up to a specific amount without extra sign-off — a phased payment may fall under it.
They haven't pushed back on your qualifications — only on writing the full check at once.

steps.title: Offer the split before they ask
steps.desc: Say: 'If timing is the issue, I can split this into three payments. The total stays the same.'

steps.title: Set a clear schedule
steps.desc: Propose: 25% to start, 25% at midpoint, 50% on delivery. Send it in writing the same day.

steps.title: Confirm the total is unchanged
steps.desc: Say explicitly: 'The total is [X]. We're just spreading when it hits your account.'

cards.script: "If timing is the issue, I can split this into three payments. The total stays at [X] — we're just changing when it lands."
cards.counter:
Someone offering you a payment plan while holding the full total.
• Calculate the real cost of waiting: your time, delayed cash, and other options you close off by staying.
• A 90-day payment schedule costs you something — factor that in before agreeing.
• Ask if the total can move in exchange for the extended schedule you're being asked to take.
cards.insight: The first payment is the real close — once they've paid once, they're pulled toward finishing. A 25% deposit buys commitment, not just cash.

cards.title: Phase the Work Across Two Budget Cycles
cards.hook: This quarter has no budget. Next quarter might. Split the project and start now.
cards.truth:
Budget cycles kill projects that are too large to approve in one go.
• A phased project lets them approve Phase 1 now and Phase 2 next cycle — each within their approval limit.
• You start the relationship, prove your value, and make Phase 2 the obvious next step.
• This works especially well when the person you're talking to has a small approval amount.
cards.remember: Get paid for Phase 1 now. Let Phase 2 sell itself after.
cards.theySee: A consultant drawing a line between two project phases on a page and asking which one fits this quarter's budget.

signals.t: They mention Q1 or a fiscal year reset — they're already thinking in budget cycles.
They get excited about one specific part of your offer — that's your Phase 1.
They say they can approve up to a certain amount without extra sign-off — design Phase 1 to fit under it.
They describe goals six to twelve months out — they expect to make multiple decisions over time.

steps.title: Find the starting piece
steps.desc: Identify the part of your offer they responded to most. That's Phase 1.

steps.title: Price Phase 1 under their limit
steps.desc: If they can approve [X] without extra sign-off, price Phase 1 at [X] or just under it.

steps.title: Name Phase 2 without pitching it
steps.desc: Say: 'Phase 2 makes sense after we see results from this. We can talk about it then.' Then stop.

cards.script: "Let's do Phase 1 now within your current budget. Phase 2 we can revisit next quarter once you've seen what this produces."
cards.counter:
Someone offering you a Phase 1 at a low price to get you started.
• Ask: 'What does Phase 2 cost and what triggers it?' Get the number before you agree to anything.
• Don't start work without knowing the full picture in writing.
• Whatever you charge for Phase 1 sets the rate they expect for everything that follows.
cards.insight: Phase 1 is a test — but it's also a trap if you price it too low to win the work. The rate you set on Phase 1 is the anchor for Phase 2.

cards.title: Tell Them to Budget for It Next Cycle and Call You Back
cards.hook: They can't buy now. Make sure you're the name they remember when the money opens up.
cards.truth:
Some 'no budgets' are real — and some become yes six months later with zero follow-up from anyone.
• End the conversation with a specific return date, not a vague 'stay in touch.'
• Tell them when to call, not if. That difference matters more than it looks.
• Leave a one-page summary behind — so the case is already built when they go to budget.
cards.remember: End every 'not now' with a specific date to talk again.
cards.theySee: A person wrapping up a meeting calmly with a clear next step instead of pushing harder or leaving frustrated.

signals.t: They say 'this is a Q3 decision' — they already know when the money will be available.
They're friendly at the end despite saying no — the door isn't actually closed.
They ask you to stay in touch — they want a reason to say yes later.
They ask for a proposal or deck to share internally — they're starting to build the internal case.

steps.title: Set the return date
steps.desc: Ask: 'When does your next budget cycle open?' Then say: 'I'll reach out the week before with what you need.'

steps.title: Leave one page behind
steps.desc: Send a single-page summary after the meeting: problem, solution, price, your contact. Nothing more than that.

steps.title: Follow up exactly when you said
steps.desc: Set a calendar reminder now. Reach out on the date you named. Showing up on time is itself the close.

cards.script: "When does your next budget cycle open? I'll reach out that week with everything you need to make the case internally."
cards.counter:
Someone leaving a 'call us when budget opens' with no date attached.
• That's a polite no unless you force a specific month out of them before you leave.
• Ask: 'When specifically — what month does that happen?'
• If they won't name a date, accept the real answer and move your time elsewhere.
cards.insight: Most follow-up loses deals not because the answer changed but because nobody showed up at the right moment. The name in their inbox when budget opens wins.

cards.title: Anchor High Before They Name Their Number
cards.hook: Whoever names a number first sets the center of gravity. Make sure it's you.
cards.truth:
The first number in a negotiation pulls all the others toward it. Documented and almost always ignored.
• Anchor at the high end before they quote a budget cap or a market rate.
• Even an obviously high number shifts the final result upward — the other side counters from your anchor.
• If they anchor first, you're negotiating against their number — not your value.
cards.remember: Name your number first. Every counter will be measured against it.
cards.theySee: Someone who leads with a price confidently before being asked, without a long setup or apology.

signals.t: They're about to ask for your number — anchor before they set a range.
They ask 'what does something like this typically run?' — your next sentence is your anchor.
They mention what others charge — they're checking if you're near it. Anchor above it.
They've delayed the money conversation — they're about to name a cap.

steps.title: Set your anchor before the meeting
steps.desc: Write it down: 30–50% above your minimum acceptable price. That's your opening number.

steps.title: Drop it before they ask
steps.desc: Say: 'Projects like this typically run between [X] and [Y] depending on scope.' Work it in naturally.

steps.title: Let them react
steps.desc: Their reaction tells you where they actually are. Negotiate toward your real number, not from theirs.

cards.script: "Projects like this typically run between [X] and [Y] depending on what we want to accomplish."
cards.counter:
Someone anchoring high before you've named a number.
• Don't react emotionally — that's the move working on you exactly as designed.
• Say: 'That's a reference point. What's actually in scope here?' Separate anchor from negotiation.
• Name your counter with confidence. Don't let their number become your ceiling.
cards.insight: The real gap isn't between your anchor and their counter — it's between your anchor and your walk-away number. Know the second one before you say the first.

cards.title: Walk Away When the Budget Story Never Changes
cards.hook: They've said 'no budget' three times with no details attached. The third time isn't a negotiation — it's a dismissal.
cards.truth:
Some 'no budget' situations are real dead ends. Staying too long costs more than leaving early.
• A real budget constraint has specifics — dates, amounts, approval chains. A fake one stays vague no matter what you ask.
• Walking away early preserves your position. Begging for a yes kills it permanently.
• The name that left without chasing gets called back. The name that stayed and pushed doesn't.
cards.principle: BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement
cards.remember: Decide your walk-away point before you walk in. Leave when you hit it.
cards.theySee: A person packing up calmly and naming one clear condition for returning, without arguing or over-explaining anything.

signals.t: You've asked directly three times and still have no real number or date — this is a real no.
Three meetings in and you've never spoken to whoever approves — they're not serious.
Every meeting the project gets smaller with no price discussion — they want free work.
Weeks go by, you send follow-ups, nothing changes — the interest was never real.

steps.title: Set your limit before you go in
steps.desc: Decide in advance: 'If I don't have a real number and a decision date by the end of this meeting, I'm done.'

steps.title: Name your condition
steps.desc: Say: 'I need a real budget range and a decision date to move forward. If that's not possible, I understand.'

steps.title: Leave without chasing
steps.desc: Say: 'When that changes, reach out.' Then stop following up completely. Let the silence work for you.

cards.script: "I need a real budget figure and a timeline to move forward. If that's not possible right now, I understand — reach out when things change."
cards.counter:
Someone walking away to force your hand into moving first.
• Don't chase. Let them go and give it 48 hours before you do anything.
• If they come back in two days, they were bluffing — and now you know your position is stronger.
• If they don't come back, you learned what the deal was actually worth to them.
cards.insight: The walk works until you need the deal more than they do — and they can usually tell. Your real walk-away power comes from having other options lined up before you sit down.
